conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: What part of the GI tract does Crohn's disease affect?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: Any part from mouth to anus; classically terminal ileum. Skip lesions with normal bowel in between.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: What is the depth of inflammation in Crohn's?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: Transmural (full thickness), predisposing to fistulae, strictures and abscesses.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: EXAM PEARL: What distinguishes Crohn's from UC histologically?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back:
• Crohn's: non-caseating granulomas, transmural inflammation, skip lesions
  • UC: continuous mucosal/submucosal inflammation, crypt abscesses, no granulomas

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: What is the characteristic endoscopic appearance of Crohn's?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back:
• Cobblestoning
  • deep linear ulcers
  • skip lesions
  • strictures

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: What smoking association does Crohn's have?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: Smoking WORSENS Crohn's (opposite to UC where it is protective).

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: Which antibody is more associated with Crohn's?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: ASCA (anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies) positive; pANCA usually negative.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: What is the first-line investigation to assess small bowel Crohn's?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: MRI enterography (or capsule endoscopy if no stricture).

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: What blood marker reflects disease activity in Crohn's?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: Faecal calprotectin (raised), CRP, ESR; low albumin and anaemia in active disease.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: How is a flare of Crohn's induced into remission?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: Glucocorticoids (oral prednisolone or budesonide for ileocaecal disease) first line.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: What is used for maintenance of remission in Crohn's?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: Azathioprine or mercaptopurine; methotrexate as alternative.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: EXAM PEARL: What must you check before starting azathioprine?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: TPMT activity (deficiency risks severe myelosuppression).

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: What biologics are used in Crohn's?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: Anti-TNF (infliximab, adalimumab); also ustekinumab, vedolizumab.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: What is a common perianal complication of Crohn's?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: Perianal fistula and abscess; treated with infliximab +/- surgery, seton drainage.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: What nutritional deficiency is classic in terminal ileal Crohn's?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: B12 deficiency (terminal ileum absorbs B12); also bile salt malabsorption causing diarrhoea.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: What surgical principle applies in Crohn's?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: Surgery is NOT curative; conserve bowel. Indicated for strictures, fistulae, failed medical therapy.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: What extra-intestinal manifestation correlates with bowel activity?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: Erythema nodosum and peripheral arthritis (correlate with flares).

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: Name an extra-intestinal manifestation NOT related to disease activity.
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back:
• Primary sclerosing cholangitis
  • ankylosing spondylitis
  • uveitis (variable)

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: What complication causes obstructive symptoms in Crohn's?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: Fibrotic strictures leading to small bowel obstruction.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: Why are renal stones common in Crohn's?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: Fat malabsorption → calcium binds fat → oxalate absorbed → calcium oxalate stones (enteric hyperoxaluria).

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: What is the peak age of onset of Crohn's?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: Bimodal: 15-30 years and a smaller peak 60-80 years.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: What part of the bowel does UC affect?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: Colon only; starts in rectum and extends proximally in a continuous fashion. Never affects beyond ileocaecal valve (except backwash ileitis).

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: What is the depth of inflammation in UC?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: Mucosa and submucosa only (not transmural).

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the smoking relationship in UC?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: Smoking is PROTECTIVE in UC; stopping smoking can trigger flares.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: What antibody is associated with UC?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: pANCA positive (ASCA negative).

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: What is the classic presenting symptom of UC?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: Bloody diarrhoea with mucus, urgency, tenesmus.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: What histology is seen in UC?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back:
• Crypt abscesses
  • goblet cell depletion
  • continuous mucosal inflammation
  • no granulomas

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: What endoscopic findings occur in UC?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back:
• Continuous erythema
  • friable mucosa
  • loss of vascular pattern
  • pseudopolyps

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: What is toxic megacolon?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: Acute colonic dilatation >6cm with systemic toxicity; risk of perforation. Life-threatening UC complication.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: How is mild-moderate UC induced into remission?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: Topical and/or oral aminosalicylates (mesalazine); add oral steroids if inadequate.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: How is acute severe UC managed?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: IV hydrocortisone; if no response in 72h, IV ciclosporin or infliximab, consider colectomy.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: What score assesses acute severe UC?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: Truelove and Witts criteria (stool frequency, blood, fever, tachycardia, anaemia, ESR).

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: What is used for maintenance in UC?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: Aminosalicylates (mesalazine) first-line; azathioprine if relapsing.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: What surgery is curative for UC?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: Total colectomy (with ileostomy or ileal pouch-anal anastomosis).

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: What hepatobiliary condition is strongly linked to UC?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC).

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: Why do UC patients need colonoscopic surveillance?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: Increased colorectal cancer risk (related to duration and extent); surveillance from ~10 years.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: EXAM PEARL: How to distinguish UC from Crohn's on barium?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back:
• UC: lead-pipe colon (loss of haustra)
  • Crohn's: string sign, skip lesions, cobblestoning

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: What is the most common extent of UC at diagnosis?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: Proctitis or left-sided colitis common; pancolitis in a minority.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: What is backwash ileitis?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: Mild inflammation of terminal ileum in pancolitis due to incompetent ileocaecal valve.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: What electrolyte abnormality occurs in severe UC?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: Hypokalaemia from diarrhoea (also hypoalbuminaemia, anaemia).

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.front: What imaging is avoided in acute severe colitis and why?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.back: Colonoscopy with full bowel prep avoided due to perforation/toxic megacolon risk; use flexi-sig cautiously.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.question: A 24-year-old smoker presents with 3 months of right iliac fossa pain, non-bloody diarrhoea, weight loss, and perianal skin tags. CRP is 68. Colonoscopy shows deep ulcers with skip lesions and cobblestone mucosa in the terminal ileum. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.explanation: Crohn's disease: young smoker + RIF pain + non-bloody diarrhoea + perianal disease (skin tags) + skip lesions + cobblestone mucosa + terminal ileum involvement + deep ulcers + raised CRP. UC: rectal involvement + bloody diarrhoea + continuous disease. Smoking is a risk factor for Crohn's but protective in UC.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.question: A patient with Crohn's disease develops a complex perianal fistula. What is the initial investigation and first-line management?
options: MRI pelvis to assess fistula anatomy, then draining seton suture for complex fistulae
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.explanation: Perianal fistulae: MRI pelvis first to delineate anatomy (high vs low fistula). Simple fistula: oral metronidazole. Complex fistula (passes through sphincter muscles): draining seton suture (surgical thread through fistula tract to allow drainage and gradual fibrous healing). Infliximab for refractory fistulating Crohn's.
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.answer: MRI pelvis to assess fistula anatomy, then draining seton suture for complex fistulae

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.question: A 24-year-old smoker presents with chronic RLQ pain, weight loss and non-bloody diarrhoea. Colonoscopy shows skip lesions and cobblestoning. Most likely diagnosis?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.explanation: Skip lesions, cobblestoning, terminal ileal involvement and smoking association are classic for Crohn's. UC is continuous and rectum-up. Coeliac and IBS do not cause cobblestoning. TB is possible but less likely without exposure.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.question: Which histological feature is most specific for Crohn's disease?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.explanation: Non-caseating granulomas with transmural inflammation are characteristic of Crohn's. Crypt abscesses, continuous inflammation and pseudopolyps favour UC. Caseating granulomas suggest TB.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.question: Which lifestyle factor worsens Crohn's disease?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.explanation: Smoking worsens Crohn's and increases relapse/surgery. In UC smoking is protective. The others are not established disease-modifiers in Crohn's.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.question: First-line agent to induce remission in a Crohn's flare?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.explanation: Steroids induce remission. Azathioprine/methotrexate are maintenance agents (slow onset). Infliximab is reserved for refractory/fistulising disease. Mesalazine has limited efficacy in Crohn's.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.question: Before starting azathioprine in Crohn's, which test is essential?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.explanation: TPMT deficiency predisposes to life-threatening myelosuppression with azathioprine. The others are not pre-treatment safety checks for thiopurines.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.question: A patient with terminal ileal Crohn's develops macrocytic anaemia. Most likely cause?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.explanation: Terminal ileum absorbs B12; its disease/resection causes B12 deficiency (macrocytic). Iron deficiency is microcytic. Folate deficiency is possible but B12 is the classic ileal association.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.question: Most appropriate investigation to assess small bowel Crohn's extent?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.explanation: MR enterography images the small bowel without radiation. Sigmoidoscopy reaches only the distal colon. The others do not assess small bowel mucosa adequately.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.question: A 30-year-old with Crohn's develops recurrent perianal discharge and pain. Best imaging?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.explanation: MRI pelvis defines perianal fistula tracts. Plain films and CT chest are irrelevant; barium enema does not characterise fistulae well.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.question: Which antibody profile favours Crohn's over UC?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.explanation: ASCA+/pANCA- favours Crohn's; the reverse favours UC. Anti-dsDNA (lupus), anti-CCP (RA) and AMA (PBC) are unrelated.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.question: Which is true about surgery in Crohn's disease?
options: It is first-line for all patients
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.explanation: Crohn's surgery treats complications but recurrence is common, so bowel is conserved. UC by contrast can be cured by colectomy.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.question: A patient with severe UC is admitted and started on IV hydrocortisone 100mg QDS. After 4 days there is no improvement. What is the next management step?
options: Continue for a further 7 days before deciding
Start oral mesalazine as rescue therapy
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.explanation: Severe UC not responding to IV hydrocortisone at 72–96 hours = medical rescue therapy. Options: IV ciclosporin (calcineurin inhibitor) OR infliximab (anti-TNF). Both are second-line options that may avoid emergency colectomy. If these fail → surgical colectomy. This is Oxford criteria decision point.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.question: Which cancer risk is most elevated in a patient with extensive UC of 15 years duration compared to the general population?
options: Colorectal cancer — increased risk with duration and extent of colitis
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.explanation: Colorectal cancer: major risk in UC (higher than Crohn's due to continuous disease). Risk increases with disease extent, duration (especially >8–10 years), and severity. Surveillance colonoscopy recommended after 8–10 years of extensive UC. PSC also significantly increases CRC risk in UC patients.
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.answer: Colorectal cancer — increased risk with duration and extent of colitis

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.question: A 28-year-old non-smoker presents with bloody diarrhoea, urgency and tenesmus. Colonoscopy shows continuous inflammation from rectum. Diagnosis?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.explanation: Continuous rectal-onset inflammation with bloody diarrhoea in a non-smoker is classic UC. Crohn's has skip lesions and is worsened by smoking. The others do not fit the continuous endoscopic pattern.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.question: Which is protective against ulcerative colitis?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.explanation: Smoking is protective in UC (and worsens Crohn's). NSAIDs can trigger flares. Appendicectomy is protective only if done young. The others have no protective role.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.question: A patient with severe UC has abdominal distension; AXR shows transverse colon dilated to 7cm with systemic toxicity. Diagnosis?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.explanation: Colonic dilatation >6cm with toxicity in UC is toxic megacolon, risking perforation. Volvulus shows coffee-bean sign; SBO involves small bowel; ileus/pseudo-obstruction lack the toxic colitis context.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.question: First-line treatment for mild-moderate left-sided UC?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.explanation: Topical/oral mesalazine is first-line. Ciclosporin/infliximab are for acute severe steroid-refractory disease. Colectomy is for refractory/complicated disease. Methotrexate is not standard in UC.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.question: A patient with acute severe UC shows no response to 72h IV hydrocortisone. Next step?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.explanation: Failure of IV steroids at 72h warrants rescue therapy (ciclosporin/infliximab) or colectomy. Antimotility agents risk toxic megacolon and are contraindicated.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.question: Which extra-intestinal/hepatobiliary disease is most associated with UC?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.explanation: PSC has a strong association with UC. PBC associates with other autoimmune conditions; the others have no specific UC link.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.question: Which histological feature favours UC over Crohn's?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.explanation: Crypt abscesses with continuous mucosal inflammation and no granulomas indicate UC. Granulomas, transmural change, skip lesions and fistulae indicate Crohn's.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.question: What is the definitive curative treatment for ulcerative colitis?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.explanation: Because UC is confined to the colon, total colectomy is curative. Medical therapies control but do not cure. This contrasts with Crohn's where surgery is not curative.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.question: Which antibody pattern favours UC?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.explanation: pANCA+/ASCA- favours UC; the reverse favours Crohn's. AMA is PBC, ASMA is autoimmune hepatitis, anti-tTG is coeliac.

conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.question: Why do long-standing UC patients require colonoscopic surveillance?
conditions__GASTROENTEROLOGY / HEPATOLOG.explanation: Chronic colonic inflammation raises colorectal cancer risk proportional to duration/extent, mandating surveillance. The other listed reasons relate more to Crohn's complications.
